findings.topic: The 'new popular strategy' the user recalls is almost certainly Lazy Leveling / Dostoevsky (Dayan & Idreos, SIGMOD'18)
findings.detail: Lazy Leveling is the headline modern result and the most-cited 'new' compaction idea of the last decade. Mechanism: it is a hybrid that applies TIERING at every level except the largest, and LEVELING only at the largest level. Rationale (disk-centric): in a leveled tree the largest level holds ~90% of the data, so eagerly merge-sorting the small upper levels (leveling everywhere) buys almost no read/space benefit but pays most of the write-amplification cost. Lazy leveling removes that 'superfluous merging': it improves worst-case UPDATE cost while keeping the SAME bounds on point-lookup, long-range-lookup, and space. It costs more on SHORT range lookups (more runs to merge in the upper, now-tiered levels). The paper also introduces Fluid LSM-tree (a continuous knob between tiering and leveling per level) and the Dostoevsky auto-tuner that picks the Fluid point maximizing throughput under a space-amp constraint. KEY: every benefit it delivers is denominated in DISK write-amplification (flash wear / I/O bandwidth). Timelog has NO disk, so the quantity lazy leveling minimizes does not exist in the form the paper assumes.

findings.topic: The RUM conjecture is the lens that explains why most of these tricks do NOT transfer to Timelog
findings.detail: RUM (Athanassoulis et al., EDBT'16): any access method trades off Read overhead, Update overhead, and Memory/space overhead — you can bound two but the third suffers. Every compaction paper below is an exercise in re-balancing R/U/M for a DISK-resident store where U (write-amp) directly equals flash wear + I/O bandwidth, and M (space-amp) equals expensive SSD capacity. Timelog changes the constants drastically: U is in-memory memcpy + page-array rebuild + refcount churn (cheap, no durability fsync, no wear), and M is RAM (precious, but compaction transients are bounded by window granularity, not by 'keep old+new copy of the whole largest level'). So Timelog already sits at a different RUM corner than any disk LSM. This is the single most important framing for deciding what to port: optimize Timelog for query latency (R) and RAM transient (M), NOT for write-amp (U), because U is nearly free here.

findings.topic: Timelog's actual compaction is already a Tiered-L0 + Leveled-L1 + TWCS hybrid
findings.detail: Verified in core/src/maint/tl_compaction.c. Trigger: tl_compact_needed fires when l0_count >= max_delta_segments (default 8) OR delete_debt crosses threshold (lines 372-383). Selection: tl__compact_select_greedy (line 553) greedily takes L0 segments in manifest order up to three caps (max_inputs, max_compaction_windows, compaction_target_bytes), then tl__compact_select_l1 (line 451) pulls in EVERY L1 segment whose WINDOW overlaps the output range and rewrites it. Output is partitioned into non-overlapping time windows (L1 invariant). Structurally this is exactly RocksDB '1-leveling' (tiering at the delta/L0 tier, leveling at L1) crossed with Cassandra TWCS (L1 = non-overlapping fixed/adaptive TIME windows). Conclusion: Timelog has ALREADY independently arrived at the hybrid the literature converged on. There is no 'tiering everywhere but the top' to add — it has exactly two persistent tiers (overlapping L0, non-overlapping L1).

findings.topic: Lazy Leveling specifically does NOT transfer — Timelog's 'levels' are time windows, not size tiers
findings.detail: Lazy leveling's whole premise is a size-ratio cascade L0<L1<...<Ln where Ln holds ~90% of data and is the expensive thing to keep leveled. Timelog's L1 is NOT a size cascade — it is a flat partition of the time domain into non-overlapping windows (TWCS-like), and there is no L2/L3/.../Ln to 'lazily tier'. The single dial Timelog exposes that is analogous to the tiering<->leveling spectrum is max_delta_segments: raising it lets more overlapping L0 runs accumulate before compaction (more tiering-like: lower write-amp, higher query fan-in), lowering it forces eager merge into L1 (more leveling-like: higher write-amp, lower query fan-in). That dial already exists. Porting 'lazy leveling' would mean adding intermediate non-overlapping levels (L2, L3) with a size ratio — which fights the time-window model and buys nothing because the write-amp it saves is in-memory and nearly free. VERDICT: inapplicable as a structural change; the useful intuition (don't over-merge cheap small runs) is already captured by max_delta_segments.

findings.topic: Size-Tiered (STCS) and Leveled (LCS) classics — already on the spectrum Timelog spans
findings.detail: STCS (Cassandra default): compact when N similar-sized SSTables accumulate; low write-amp, high read-amp and high space-amp (up to ~2x transient because it merges large equal tiers). LCS: fixed-size SSTables in levels, each level non-overlapping and 10x prior; low read-amp and bounded space-amp, but write-amp commonly >10 (ScyllaDB measured leveled write-amp can be 20-30x). Timelog's L0 behaves like a small bounded STCS tier (cap = max_delta_segments) and L1 behaves like LCS's non-overlap-per-level guarantee but partitioned by TIME instead of by size+key-range. Neither pure STCS nor pure LCS is worth adopting wholesale: Timelog already takes the bounded-tier idea from STCS and the non-overlap idea from LCS. The one LCS property Timelog does NOT have and could consider is multiple leveled levels — but see the lazy-leveling verdict: no disk WA to save.

findings.topic: TWCS (Time-Window Compaction) — the strategy Timelog most resembles, and the source of its best untapped idea
findings.detail: Cassandra TWCS: bucket SSTables by time window; compact WITHIN a window using STCS; never cross-compact between windows; whole windows can be dropped cheaply (TTL/expiry) and 'fully expired SSTables drop more efficiently'. Recommended to size windows so ~20-30 exist. Timelog's L1 = non-overlapping time windows IS TWCS's core structure. The transferable, currently-underused TWCS idea: WHOLE-WINDOW DROP. Because L1 windows are non-overlapping in time, a query range or a delete/tombstone that fully covers a window means that entire L1 segment can be dropped or skipped without a merge. TWCS also warns about OOO/late-arriving data smearing across windows — which is precisely Timelog's OOO mini-LSM concern. This is the closest real-world analog and the most fruitful to mine.

findings.topic: RocksDB Universal vs Leveled — Universal's space-amp doubling is a dealbreaker in RAM
findings.detail: RocksDB Universal (= Tiered): merges all runs in a level into the next without rewriting existing runs; per-level write-amp = 1 (lowest write-amp), but read-amp higher and space-amp unbounded — 'space usage effectively doubles during compaction' and RocksDB recommends sharding to mitigate. Leveled: 'some-to-some', rewrites only overlapping data, bounds space-amp but write-amp 20-30x. Tiered+Leveled (RocksDB's actual default, '1-leveling'): tiering at L0, leveling above — less write-amp than leveled, less space-amp than tiered. For Timelog (in RAM): Universal's write-amp win is irrelevant (no disk), and its space-amp DOUBLING is actively harmful because RAM is the scarce resource. Leveled's write-amp penalty is irrelevant (no disk). So the RocksDB lesson that DOES apply is the Tiered+Leveled hybrid shape — which Timelog already implements. Universal is the one to explicitly reject for an in-memory engine.

findings.topic: Monkey (Bloom-filter allocation) — entirely inapplicable to Timelog
findings.detail: Monkey (Dayan, Athanassoulis, Idreos, SIGMOD'17 / TODS'18): point-lookup cost is proportional to the SUM of per-level Bloom-filter false-positive rates; allocate more bits-per-element to smaller (upper) levels and fewer to the large bottom level to minimize that sum, cutting lookup latency 50-80%. This is purely about POINT lookups on a KEY via Bloom filters. Timelog is a TIME-RANGE index: it answers [t1,t2) via fence pointers + binary search (lower_bound) within sorted pages, and L1 windows are non-overlapping so a timestamp maps to at most one L1 window. There are NO Bloom filters and no point-key existence test to optimize. Monkey is inapplicable; the analogous 'skip work using metadata' role is already played by fence pointers + window bounds.

findings.topic: Spooky (VLDB'22) and partial-vs-full merge — the ONE idea genuinely worth prototyping, in spirit
findings.detail: Spooky (Dayan et al., VLDB'22) attacks compaction GRANULARITY: Full Merge (compact a whole level at once) gives low write-amp but needs ~2x space transiently (old + new copy of the largest level coexist until done); Partial Merge (compact small overlapping file groups) bounds the transient space but pays excessive write-amp. Spooky partitions data by FILE LIFETIME / preorders so files in a partition expire together, getting low write-amp AND bounded space transient. Mapped to Timelog: Timelog's compaction currently rewrites ALL window-overlapping L1 segments in one merge (tl__compact_select_l1), so a wide L0 spread can rewrite many L1 windows and transiently hold old+new copies — a Full-Merge-style RAM spike. The transferable idea is GRANULAR / per-window compaction: merge L0 into each overlapping L1 window INDEPENDENTLY (or in small batches), bounding peak RAM transient to one window's worth instead of the whole overlapping span. This directly targets Timelog's scarce resource (RAM M-overhead), is consistent with the non-overlapping-window invariant, and the existing max_compaction_windows / compaction_target_bytes caps are already the seam to do it.

findings.topic: ScyllaDB Incremental Compaction (ICS) + Space-Amplification-Goal (SAG) — partially transferable
findings.detail: ScyllaDB ICS replaces STCS's big sorted runs with sequences of smaller fixed-size 'SSTable runs', so cross-tier compaction works in increments and never needs the full 2x transient of merging two huge tiers — directly cutting the peak space transient. SAG (Space Amplification Goal, 1.0-2.0) triggers cross-tier compaction once the second-largest tier reaches a fraction of the largest, continuously bounding space-amp; closer to 1.0 = more write-amp + less space-amp. The TRANSFERABLE part for Timelog is the INCREMENTAL/bounded-transient idea (same family as Spooky's granularity fix): bound the RAM held during a compaction by chunking the merge. The SAG dial concept is less relevant — Timelog's 'space amplification' from overwrites is modeled instead via delete_debt_threshold (tombstone-driven), which already serves the same 'compact to reclaim space when debt is high' role.

findings.topic: 'k-LSM' is a false lead — it is a concurrent priority queue, not a compaction strategy
findings.detail: The 'k-LSM' in the literature (Wimmer et al., PPoPP'15, 'The Lock-free k-LSM Relaxed Priority Queue') is a lock-free RELAXED PRIORITY QUEUE built from a logarithmic stack of sorted arrays that borrows the LSM SHAPE for delete-min scalability. It relaxes linearization (delete-min may return any of the k+1 smallest keys). It has nothing to do with LSM compaction policy and is not a storage-engine technique. Flag so it is not chased. (The lock-free-stack/Treiber idea it shares with Timelog's retired-handle queue is already present in the binding's drop path.)

findings.topic: FluidLSM and the broader design-space framing
findings.detail: Fluid LSM-tree (the generalization inside the Dostoevsky paper) parameterizes the entire tiering<->leveling continuum with two knobs: the size ratio T and, per level, how many runs accumulate before merging (Z at the largest level, K elsewhere). Lazy leveling is the special point K=T-1 (tier) everywhere, Z=1 (level) at the bottom. Sarkar et al.'s 'Constructing and Analyzing the LSM Compaction Design Space' (VLDB'21) generalizes this further into ~primitive dimensions (trigger, granularity, data movement, layout). The actionable takeaway for Timelog: its design space is already collapsed to two structural tiers (L0 overlapping, L1 time-windowed non-overlapping) plus the max_delta_segments dial — most Fluid points are unreachable/irrelevant because there is no multi-level size cascade and no disk WA to trade. The only Fluid dimension with headroom is GRANULARITY (Spooky/ICS axis), not the tiering<->leveling axis.

recommendations.action: Prototype GRANULAR / per-window L1 compaction (the Spooky/ICS idea): instead of merging all window-overlapping L1 segments in one off-lock pass, split the merge so it processes one L1 window (or a small bounded batch) at a time, bounding peak RAM transient to roughly one window of old+new instead of the whole overlapping span. Reuse the existing max_compaction_windows / compaction_target_bytes caps in tl__compact_select_greedy as the chunking seam.
recommendations.rationale: This is the ONE idea from the modern frontier that targets Timelog's actually-scarce resource (RAM, the M in RUM) rather than disk write-amp (which is nearly free in-memory). Today a wide L0 timestamp spread can pull in many L1 windows (tl__compact_select_l1) and transiently hold old+new copies — a Full-Merge-style RAM spike. Granular merge bounds that spike while preserving the non-overlapping-window invariant.
recommendations.expected_signal: Peak RSS during compaction (transient allocation high-water) drops materially on wide-spread / bulk-OOO workloads; compactions_total may rise (more, smaller publishes) but compaction_retries / compaction_publish_ebusy should not regress, and query p99 during compaction improves.

recommendations.action: Implement WHOLE-WINDOW DROP / skip for L1 (the TWCS expiry idea): when a tombstone interval (or delete range) fully covers an L1 window's [window_start, window_end), drop that L1 segment outright instead of merging it; and at query time, skip L1 windows fully outside [t1,t2). Wire it into the delete_debt path so fully-covered windows count as cheap reclaim.
recommendations.rationale: L1 non-overlap by TIME makes whole-segment drop trivially correct (no key-range ambiguity) — the exact property TWCS exploits for 'fully expired SSTables drop efficiently'. It converts a merge into an O(1) manifest edit, the cheapest possible reclaim, and is a natural fit for TTL/retention-style deletes which are the dominant delete shape for a time index.
recommendations.expected_signal: For delete/TTL-heavy workloads: compactions_total and merged record volume drop (drops replace merges); tombstone_count and segments_l1 fall faster; delete-debt-triggered compaction frequency decreases.

recommendations.action: Document max_delta_segments explicitly as the tiering<->leveling dial and the chosen RUM posture (optimize R and RAM-M, treat write-amp U as free) in docs/internals/components/compaction-and-maintenance.md, citing the convergence with RocksDB 1-leveling and Cassandra TWCS.
recommendations.rationale: The research shows Timelog already independently lands on the industry-consensus hybrid (Tiered-L0 + Leveled/TWCS-L1). Naming this and the in-memory RUM inversion prevents future contributors from chasing disk-oriented wins (lazy leveling extra levels, Universal compaction, Monkey Bloom filters) that the analysis shows are inapplicable.
recommendations.expected_signal: Qualitative: fewer misdirected compaction proposals; the dial's effect on l0_count vs query fan-in becomes a documented, testable contract.

recommendations.action: Explicitly REJECT (in design notes, do not build): RocksDB Universal/Tiered compaction (its space-amp doubling is harmful in RAM), Monkey Bloom-filter allocation (no point-key existence test; Timelog is a time-range index with fence pointers), structural lazy-leveling extra non-overlapping levels (no size cascade, no disk WA to save), and anything derived from 'k-LSM' (it is a priority queue, not a compaction policy).
recommendations.rationale: Each was evaluated against Timelog's constraints (in-memory, time-windowed non-overlapping L1, range-only queries) and fails for a concrete reason. Recording the rejection rationale is as valuable as the adoption, given the user specifically asked which are inapplicable and why.
recommendations.expected_signal: N/A (decision record). Prevents wasted prototyping effort; keeps the maintenance surface minimal.

findings.topic: stats() taxonomy: which fields are CUMULATIVE counters vs INSTANTANEOUS gauges (decides every metric formula)
findings.detail: Mixing the two is the #1 methodology trap. CUMULATIVE-since-open (read as deltas across a measurement window, monotonic, atomic counters): operational.{seals_total, flushes_total, compactions_total, compaction_retries, compaction_publish_ebusy, backpressure_waits, ooo_budget_hits} and compaction_selection.{select_calls, select_l0_inputs, select_l1_inputs, select_no_work} and adaptive.flush_count. INSTANTANEOUS GAUGES recomputed per call against a fresh pinned snapshot (NOT cumulative): storage.{segments_l0, segments_l1, pages_total, records_estimate, tombstone_count, min_ts, max_ts} and memtable.{active_records, ooo_records, sealed_runs} and adaptive.{window, ewma_density}. Confirmed in core: counters use tl_atomic_inc/fetch_add (tl_compaction.c:710,717-720,1428), gauges are summed live per call in tl_stats() (tl_timelog.c:2012-2106). Harness rule: snapshot the full dict before and after each phase; subtract counters, read gauges only at quiescence.

findings.topic: WRITE AMPLIFICATION: best available proxy is select_l1_inputs growth, NOT compactions_total or pages_total churn
findings.detail: stats() exposes no bytes-rewritten. The soundest proxy is the cumulative count of SEGMENTS fed INTO compaction merges, accumulated at selection time: compaction_selection.select_l0_inputs and select_l1_inputs (tl_compaction.c:717-720, incremented by ctx->input_l0_len / input_l1_len each successful select). Each selected L1 input is an existing non-overlapping segment that gets re-merged and rewritten — so delta(select_l1_inputs) over a run is a direct count of L1 re-writes, the dominant write-amp term in a leveled engine. PROXY WAF = (records_flushed_to_L0 + records_rewritten_by_compaction) / records_flushed_to_L0. Components measurable from Python: (a) bytes/records flushed once = sum over flushes; approximate from delta(flushes_total) x (memtable_max_bytes/16) OR exactly by tracking your own append byte total. (b) compaction rewrite volume: there is NO per-merge record count in stats, so approximate rewritten records as delta(select_l0_inputs + select_l1_inputs) x avg_segment_records, where avg_segment_records is estimated from a quiescent pages_total/segments_total x records_per_page. RANKED proxies, best to worst: (1) delta(select_l1_inputs) [pure re-write signal, cleanest knob-discriminator]; (2) (select_l0_inputs+select_l1_inputs) per compaction = merge fan-in; (3) compactions_total alone [too coarse — ignores inputs-per-compaction, misleads when max_compaction_inputs differs]; (4) pages_total time-series churn [confounded — it's a steady-state gauge that nets allocation against reclamation, cannot see transient rewrite volume]. LIMITATIONS to state in the report: select_*_inputs counts SEGMENTS not bytes/records; segment sizes vary (L0 from sealed memruns ~memtable_max_bytes, L1 up to compaction_target_bytes), so converting to bytes needs the records_per_page assumption; counter increments only on SUCCESSFUL select (st==TL_OK at tl_compaction.c:716), so EBUSY-aborted attempts are invisible — cross-check with compaction_retries/publish_ebusy.

findings.topic: SPACE AMPLIFICATION: pages_total x target_page_bytes / logical_bytes, with len() NOT usable as the logical denominator
findings.detail: Physical bytes proxy = pages_total x target_page_bytes (each page is allocated to ~target_page_bytes; records_per_page = (target_page_bytes - sizeof(tl_page_t)) / 16, where 16 = sizeof(tl_ts_t)+sizeof(tl_handle_t), tl_page.c:8-19). This counts ONLY L0+L1 segment pages — memtable/sealed runs are excluded from pages_total (tl_timelog.c:2047-2061), so it measures persisted-tier space-amp, which is what compaction controls. Logical bytes = (live logical record count) x 16. CRITICAL: do NOT use len(log) as the denominator — len() returns storage.records_estimate, itself a tombstone-aware visible-count GAUGE/proxy (python __init__.py:432-435, tl_timelog.c:2081), so SA computed as pages_records/records_estimate would be near-tautological and hide tombstone-driven bloat. Track the TRUE logical count in the harness: increment per successful append, and for delete-storm workloads subtract records whose ts falls in deleted ranges (the harness owns the data generator, so it knows exactly). Two SA numbers worth reporting: SA_physical = pages_total x target_page_bytes / (true_live_records x 16); and a tighter SA_packing = (records_estimate x 16) / (pages_total x target_page_bytes) inverted to expose page under-fill from partial-page L0 flushes. RSS cross-check: read /proc/self/statm (field 2 = resident pages x sysconf(SC_PAGESIZE)) or /proc/self/status VmRSS at quiescence; RSS includes Python heap + handle table + allocator overhead so it's an upper bound, useful for relative knob comparison, not absolute SA. Sample RSS only at quiescence after gc.collect() to avoid GC-pending object noise.

findings.topic: READ AMPLIFICATION / tail latency: query p50/p99 vs (segments_l0, segments_l1), pinned to a frozen snapshot, multiple shapes
findings.detail: Read-amp in this engine = merge fan-in K = segments_l0 + segments_l1 + memview components (active + ooo_runs + sealed). Method: at each quiescence point record (segments_l0, segments_l1, pages_total) then run a query battery and regress query latency against K. Query SHAPES (each is a distinct cost regime): (a) POINT query log.point(ts) / log[ts] — O(K log P) heap setup, isolates the per-source binary-search + heap overhead, most sensitive to segment COUNT; (b) NARROW range [t, t+w) with w ~ one page-span — dominated by K log P + small M; (c) WIDE recency range [max_ts - d, max_ts) e.g. last 1h/1d — the doc-style 'tail read', dominated by result size M and tests whether L1 windowing prunes non-overlapping segments; (d) FULL scan log.all() — pure throughput, M-dominated, K-insensitive. IMPORTANT engine detail: queries return a TimelogIter lazily (iter_create_internal builds plan+kmerge+filter, tl_timelog.c:1253); latency must be measured to FULL drain (sum(1 for _ in it) or list()), not just to iterator construction, or you measure only plan-build. COUNT: per (shape, knob-cell) run >= 2000 point queries and >= 500 range queries over randomized in-domain timestamps drawn from [min_ts, max_ts); report p50/p90/p99/p999 via numpy.percentile on the raw latency array (time.perf_counter_ns around each drained query). PIN/WARM: take ONE snapshot implicitly per query (each query call pins a fresh manifest) — to hold K constant, run the battery in maintenance='disabled' AFTER driving to a known (l0,l1) state via maint_step, so no background compaction shifts K mid-battery. Warm with >= 200 discarded queries first (CPython attr/heap warmup, branch predictor). Randomize ts order to defeat cache-locality bias. Confounder: the filter step skips tombstoned records (tl_filter), so delete-heavy states inflate per-record cost — report read-amp separately for clean vs delete-storm states.

findings.topic: COMPACTION CPU / throughput honestly: drive maintenance='disabled' + maint_step() loop for attributable timing; background mode only for end-to-end realism
findings.detail: DECISIVE finding: compact() is ASYNCHRONOUS even in manual mode — tl_compact() merely sets compact_pending and returns TL_OK without doing the merge (tl_timelog.c:1215-1221). The work is done by maint_step(), which performs exactly ONE unit (flush one sealed memrun, else advance compaction one step) and returns bool: True=work done, False/TL_EOF=no work due (tl_timelog.c:1956-2003, binding py_timelog.c:2133-2150). flush() by contrast IS synchronous and drains active+sealed to empty (tl_timelog.c:1118-1123). THEREFORE the only way to get attributable, confounder-free compaction CPU from Python is: maintenance='disabled'; ingest a phase; then `t0=perf_counter_ns(); while log.maint_step(): pass; cpu_ns=...` wrapping the drain-to-quiescence loop, and read counter deltas across it. This makes compaction CPU a clean function of the knobs because no concurrent writer/GC jitter overlaps it. Use BACKGROUND mode only to measure end-to-end ingest throughput and tail-write latency under the real worker — but then you CANNOT cleanly separate compaction CPU from append CPU (they overlap on the worker thread holding maint_mu during merge; CLAUDE.md confirms background OOO bulk is 3x slower due to merge lock contention). STEADY STATE: ingest until segments_l1 stops trending and delta(compactions_total)/delta(seals_total) stabilizes across two consecutive equal-size batches (write-amp ratio converged) — discard the first N batches as fill transient. TL_EBUSY handling: in measurement, treat compaction_publish_ebusy>0 and compaction_retries>0 as a confounder flag, not an error — they mean the manifest changed under publish (background writers raced); a clean manual-mode run should show both = 0. For background runs, log them per phase and exclude phases where publish_ebusy spiked. Use time.thread_time_ns() (per-thread CPU) for the manual drain loop to exclude sleep; use perf_counter_ns() wall for end-to-end. Prefer process isolation per knob-cell (subprocess) so the background thread + handle table from a prior cell can't leak state.

findings.topic: WORKLOADS (doc_6/doc_11 style): four generators that exercise the L0->L1 path differently
findings.detail: (1) STEADY APPEND (in-order): monotonically increasing ts at fixed density (records per window). Baseline for write-amp and the leveling/tiering dial. Density chosen so each window holds ~ window_size x density records, sized vs memtable_max_bytes so seals/compactions actually fire. (2) BURSTY: alternate high-rate bursts and idle gaps; bursts force rapid seals -> L0 pileup -> compaction storms; tests max_delta_segments trigger and sealed_max_runs backpressure (watch backpressure_waits). (3) DELETE-STORM: steady append, then delete_range over large historical spans to create many tombstones; measures tombstone-driven space-amp (pages stay until compaction physically drops), delete_debt_threshold-triggered compaction, and read-amp under filtering. Track tombstone_count and the gap between records_estimate and true logical count. (4) OOO-HEAVY: ~15-20% of appends with ts < current max (mostly_ordered_default still true but inject backward ts) to exercise the OOO mini-LSM (ooo_head/ooo_runs), OOO seal cost (O(H log H)), and ooo_budget_hits; CLAUDE.md notes background mode is 3x slower here, so run OOO-heavy in BOTH maintenance modes to quantify the contention. Each workload parameterized by total_records (>= 5M to match the documented OOO profiling scale, or >= 2M for faster sweeps), density, and (for 3/4) delete_fraction/ooo_fraction. Generate timestamps deterministically from a seed so paired-seed repeats are exactly comparable.

findings.topic: CONFOUNDERS and controls: background jitter, GC, seal timing, single-shot vs paired-seed repeats
findings.detail: (a) BACKGROUND-THREAD JITTER: the worker wakes every maintenance_wakeup_ms (default 100ms, tl_timelog.c:266) and holds maint_mu during merge — overlaps and perturbs both append and query timing. Control: do all ATTRIBUTABLE write-amp/compaction-CPU measurement in maintenance='disabled' with maint_step; reserve background only for explicitly-labelled end-to-end runs, and stop_maintenance() before reading final gauges so no compaction lands between snapshot and measurement. (b) GC: handle table holds a PyObject* per live record; Py_DECREF of dropped handles happens on drain (lock-free retired stack). Control: gc.disable() during timed phases, gc.collect() once at each quiescence boundary BEFORE sampling RSS/latency, and re-enable between phases. Pin object payloads to a small interned set (e.g. reuse one object) if you want to isolate engine cost from PyObject alloc cost — but use distinct objects if you want realistic handle-table pressure; state which. (c) SEAL TIMING: seals are byte-triggered by memtable_max_bytes, so identical record COUNTS across knob-cells can yield different seal counts if record payloads differ — keep payload identical across cells and compare delta(seals_total) to confirm equal flush volume before comparing compaction. (d) REPEATS: never single-shot. Run >= 5 paired-seed repeats per knob-cell (same data seed across cells so the workload is identical; vary a separate RNG seed only for query-ts sampling). Report median + IQR, and for latency report the pooled p99 across repeats (not mean of per-run p99s). Pin to a single physical core (os.sched_setaffinity) and set the background worker expectation accordingly; disable turbo/frequency scaling if possible, else report it as a caveat. (e) PROCESS ISOLATION: run each knob-cell in a fresh subprocess to eliminate allocator fragmentation, handle-table residue, and warm-cache carryover between cells. (f) FRESH-SNAPSHOT cost: every stats()/len() call pins a manifest and recomputes gauges by summing segments (O(pages+tombstones)) — do NOT call stats() inside the timed query loop; sample it only at phase boundaries.

recommendations.action: Build the harness around a strict phase protocol: SUBPROCESS per knob-cell -> gc.disable -> set affinity -> ingest workload from fixed data-seed -> drive to quiescence (flush() then `while maint_step(): pass` in maintenance='disabled') -> gc.collect() -> snapshot stats() + /proc RSS -> run query battery -> snapshot stats() again. Capture the FULL stats() dict at every phase boundary as JSON for offline analysis. Use time.thread_time_ns() for the maint_step drain (compaction CPU) and time.perf_counter_ns() per drained query for latency.
recommendations.rationale: Manual mode + maint_step drain is the ONLY way to get compaction CPU and write-amp attributable to knobs without background-thread/GC jitter (compact() is async; only maint_step does synchronous work and signals quiescence via False). Subprocess isolation kills cross-cell allocator/handle-table carryover.
recommendations.expected_signal: compaction CPU (thread_time during drain) and write-amp proxy become low-variance across paired-seed repeats (IQR shrinks markedly vs a background-mode run); compaction_publish_ebusy and compaction_retries read 0 in manual cells, confirming no race confound.

recommendations.action: Define the write-amp metric as PROXY_WAF = 1 + delta(select_l0_inputs + select_l1_inputs) x avg_segment_records / records_flushed, where records_flushed is tracked exactly by the harness (it owns appends) and avg_segment_records is measured from a quiescent pages_total/(segments_l0+segments_l1) x records_per_page. Report delta(select_l1_inputs) on its own as the primary leveling-cost discriminator. Always co-report delta(compactions_total) and delta(seals_total) so the ratio is interpretable.
recommendations.rationale: select_l1_inputs counts existing non-overlapping L1 segments re-merged (the dominant rewrite term); it is incremented per successful selection at the input granularity the engine actually controls. Pure compactions_total is too coarse and misleads across max_compaction_inputs settings.
recommendations.expected_signal: As max_delta_segments rises (more tiering), delta(compactions_total) and delta(select_l1_inputs) fall (lower write-amp) while segments_l0 at quiescence and query p99 rise (higher read-amp) — a clean, monotonic write/read tradeoff curve.

recommendations.action: Run this FIRST knob-sweep grid on the STEADY-APPEND workload (2-5M records, density tuned so >=50 windows fill): max_delta_segments in {2,4,8,16,32} (primary tiering<->leveling dial) x window_size in {0.25h,1h,4h} x target_page_bytes in {16KiB,64KiB,256KiB}, holding memtable_max_bytes=1MiB and sealed_max_runs=4. That is 45 cells; 5 paired-seed repeats each. Add a focused second pass: best max_delta_segments x compaction={max_inputs in {2,4,8,0}} x delete_debt_threshold in {0.0,0.25,0.5} on the DELETE-STORM workload. Then repeat the winning row under BOTH maintenance modes on the OOO-HEAVY workload to quantify the documented 3x background penalty.
recommendations.rationale: max_delta_segments is the single most influential knob (the L0 trigger that dials tiering vs leveling); window_size sets L1 partition granularity (read-pruning vs rewrite cost); target_page_bytes drives page packing / space-amp and per-query binary-search depth. This grid spans the dominant axes before fanning out.
recommendations.expected_signal: A Pareto frontier in (PROXY_WAF, query-p99, SA_physical) space where larger max_delta_segments and larger window_size trade write-amp down for read-amp up; the delete-storm second pass should show delete_debt_threshold>0 reclaiming pages_total (lower SA) at the cost of extra compactions_total.

recommendations.action: Compute SA_physical = pages_total x target_page_bytes / (true_live_records x 16) using a harness-tracked true_live_records (appends minus delete-covered), and explicitly DO NOT use len(log)/records_estimate as the denominator. Cross-check with VmRSS from /proc/self/status sampled at quiescence after gc.collect(). Also report SA_packing = records_estimate x 16 / (pages_total x target_page_bytes) to expose L0 page under-fill.
recommendations.rationale: len()/records_estimate is itself the tombstone-aware visible gauge; using it as the logical baseline makes SA near-tautological and hides tombstone bloat. The harness owns the generator so it can compute the true logical denominator exactly.
recommendations.expected_signal: Delete-storm cells show SA_physical spiking before compaction and dropping after delete_debt_threshold-triggered compaction; smaller target_page_bytes raises page count but improves SA_packing (less wasted tail space) at the cost of more pages and slightly higher point-query p99.

recommendations.action: For each knob-cell, run the query battery in maintenance='disabled' AFTER reaching a recorded (segments_l0, segments_l1) state, with >=2000 randomized in-domain point queries and >=500 range queries (narrow + last-d recency + full-scan), drained fully (list() the iterator), warmed with >=200 discarded queries, gc disabled. Report p50/p90/p99/p999 and regress p99 against K = segments_l0+segments_l1.
recommendations.rationale: Holding K fixed (no background compaction shifting the manifest mid-battery) is required for a valid read-amp vs segment-count regression; queries must be drained because the iterator is lazy and construction-only timing misses the merge cost.
recommendations.expected_signal: Point-query p99 grows roughly with K (more segments to heap-merge); recency-range p99 stays flat across window_size only if L1 windowing prunes non-overlapping segments effectively, isolating the read-pruning benefit of smaller windows.
